items.title: Burrill Crohn interviewed by Monk Rowe, Woodstock, New York, January 3, 2012
items.q: [INTERVIEWER] ...Evan Christopher, who’s a clarinetist we’ve had at the college, had this interesting theory...

ctx.x: So he relied on Stanley Crouch and Wynton Marsalis, and, you know, God bless both of them, they’ve done a lot for jazz and I respect Stanley as a writer and I certainly respect Wynton, because I’ve worked with Wynton and he’s got an incredible mind. But he wasn’t immersed. It’s like, you know when you’re immersed in the music from the way up you would have made a different film than you would if you had just come to it new and have to learn it while you’re doing it.

In that film, and in other places, when I read about jazz, I sometimes object to the idea that changes in music, jazz especially, are often because of social issues. To me they leave out the thing about people just experiment because they can, and because it feels good to do something new, or — Evan Christopher, who’s a clarinetist we’ve had at the college, had this interesting theory about why vibrato with the early New Orleans clarinetists, and it had to do with playing with out of tune pianos. You know, that…
Wait a minute. There’s vibrato and there’s vibrato. You have the vibrato of the clarinetist and then you have Sidney Bechet, which brought vibrato to a whole other level. He made vibrato an art form.
